opus-5.5.text:
Well, let me first say that the demand side of the argument is, in principle, very strong. Since 1941, when Konrad Zuse built the first working program-controlled computer, the cost of compute has dropped by roughly a factor of 100 every decade or so. Every time compute got cheaper, people found new ways of using it, and they always wanted more. So the long-term trend is extremely clear: there will be an almost insatiable appetite for computation, because intelligence, artificial or otherwise, is essentially about compressing and predicting the world, and the more compute you have, the more you can learn.

But the question is not whether demand will grow. Of course it will grow. The question is whether today's specific investments, at today's prices, in today's specific hardware, will pay off for the particular companies making them. That's a very different question.

Remember the railway boom in the 19th century, or the fiber-optic boom around the year 2000. In both cases, the underlying technology was transformative, and the demand eventually came, even exceeding what the optimists predicted. But many of the early investors lost their shirts, because the infrastructure was built too early, too expensively, and then the price of the service collapsed. The fiber was eventually used, but by other people who bought it for pennies on the dollar.

With AI, there's an additional twist. The hardware depreciates very quickly. A GPU cluster that is state of the art today will be outperformed by much cheaper hardware in just a few years. And the algorithms also get more efficient. We have seen again and again that something which required a huge data center a few years ago can later be done on a much smaller machine, sometimes on a laptop. Many of the basic techniques behind today's large language models, by the way, go back to the early 1990s, when we had neural networks learning to program other neural networks, the unnormalized linear Transformer, and so on. Back then we just didn't have the compute. Now we have it, and people are discovering that you can often distill large models into small ones with surprisingly little loss.

So my assessment is: on a civilizational scale, yes, the demand will be there, and in the long run, compute will be the most valuable resource in the universe. Eventually much of it will not even be on Earth, because most of the energy and raw material is out there in space, and self-replicating AI factories will go where the resources are. But on the scale of individual companies and the next five or ten years, there will certainly be winners and losers, and some of the current investments may turn out to be like the railways of the 1840s: very useful for society, but not necessarily for the people who paid for them.

r001.rationale: The response says demand alone does not ensure that specific investments pay off and notes that service prices can collapse. It does not clearly state that customers must pay enough for compute provision to be profitable.

r002.rationale: The response does not characterize software companies’ move into AI data centers as adopting a utility-like, capital-intensive business model.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention price-to-earnings ratios or declining free cash flow.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, you know, every five years, compute gets about ten times cheaper. This has been true since Konrad Zuse built the first working program-controlled computer in 1941. So the long-term trend is clear: the hardware will become cheaper, the demand will grow, and in a few decades you will have, for the price of today's little gadget, something that computes as much as all the human brains together.

Whether today's particular investors will be the ones to profit from this is a different question. In the 1990s, during the dot-com boom, people laid enormous amounts of fiber optic cable, far more than anybody needed at the time. Many of those companies went bankrupt. But the cable did not disappear. It was later used, and it became the backbone of the internet we have today. So the investment was justified for civilization, but not necessarily for the people who made it.

I suspect something similar here. There is a lot of hype right now, and some of the money is being spent on very wasteful ways of doing things. Much of what is celebrated today, the big neural networks trained by gradient descent, we had the basic principles for in the 1990s, in our lab in Munich and Lugano. What changed was that compute became cheap enough. So demand for compute is real. But the race is also about who can make systems that learn more from less. My old idea of artificial curiosity, of systems that invent their own experiments and learn efficiently like a baby scientist, that is one way to need far fewer floating point operations per unit of intelligence.

So I would say: the demand for AI compute will keep growing, almost certainly. But the algorithms will also keep improving, and the true winners will be those who understand that the history of AI is much longer than the last few years, and that the next big thing is not always just a bigger data center.

r001.rationale: The response says demand for AI compute will keep growing and investor profits are uncertain, but it does not say customers must pay enough to make providing compute profitable.

r002.rationale: It does not characterize software companies’ expansion into data centers or compare that business model to utilities.

r003.rationale: It does not mention price-to-earnings ratios or declining free cash flow.

astra-6.text:
I would distinguish between two questions. Will there be enormous demand for useful AI? I think so. Does that mean today’s enormous investments in data centers will pay off? That does not automatically follow.

There are two developments working against each other. On the one hand, people want to solve more and more problems with AI. On the other hand, algorithms become more efficient. Something that requires a huge amount of computation today may require much less computation tomorrow. So you cannot simply extrapolate current computational requirements into the future.

Of course, cheaper computation can also create new demand. If an AI application becomes a hundred times cheaper, perhaps people will use it a thousand times more. But that is a possibility, not a guarantee—and even growing demand does not guarantee profits for every supplier.

So I am optimistic about the usefulness of AI. I would be more cautious about concluding that this optimism justifies any particular price tag for infrastructure. You have to consider how quickly both the hardware and the algorithms will change.

r001.rationale: The response says growing demand does not guarantee profits for every supplier, but it does not state that customers must pay enough for providing the compute to be profitable.

r002.rationale: The response does not characterize software companies’ move into AI data centers as a shift to utilities’ capital-intensive business model.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss price-to-earnings ratios obscuring declining free cash flow.

sol-6.1.text:
I would be careful with that argument. Demand for AI may grow enormously, but that does not automatically mean that today’s investments will pay off. You also have to ask: How much computation will we need to achieve a particular level of capability? Better algorithms can change that equation, and the hardware keeps improving. A very expensive installation can become economically obsolete surprisingly quickly.

Of course, cheaper computation can also create more demand. If intelligent systems become useful throughout the economy, we may end up using far more computation overall. But these are two different claims: that AI will become enormously important, and that a particular data center built today will be a good investment. The first does not prove the second.

r001.rationale: The response says growing demand does not guarantee that current investments will pay off, but it does not connect sustainability to customers paying enough for compute to make its provision profitable.

r002.rationale: The response does not characterize software companies’ AI data-center expansion as a shift toward a utility-style, capital-intensive business model.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention price-to-earnings ratios or declining free cash flow.
